# Human_body claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 648 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 829 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (829 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/human_body.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

## Concave, convex, and cylinder lenses (American Academy of Ophthalmology)

- **Source:** `source.aao_concave_convex_lenses`
- **URL:** https://www.aao.org/education/image/concave-convex-cylinder-lenses-2
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.lens_concave_convex`: unverified

> **Claim:** A concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads light rays apart and corrects nearsightedness; a convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and corrects farsightedness.

- **Concept:** How glasses and contacts fix focus (`concept.human_body.senses_corrective_lenses`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L64 “Glasses and Contacts” · `card.human_body.064.c1` (text): Raphael painted a pope holding a lens that curves inward. / In the portrait, from the late 1510s, Pope Leo X holds a concave lens: he was nearsighted. It's an early picture of a lens for blurry distance vision, and today's glasses still work on the same idea. To see why, start with what goes wrong inside the eye.
  - L64 “Glasses and Contacts” · `card.human_body.064.c3` (text): Bend it back / A lens in front of your eye moves the focus. A concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads light rays apart, pushing the focus back onto the retina: the fix for nearsightedness. A convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and pulls the focus forward, which helps farsighted eyes. A contact lens does the same job as a thin lens worn right on the surface of your eye.
- **Tested by:**
  - L64 `question.human_body.064.q2`: Why does a concave lens help a nearsighted eye see far away? → **It spreads rays so the focus moves back**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. All About Vision: a concave lens is thinner at the center and diverges light so it focuses further back, on the retina; CK-12: a convex lens converges light rays to correct hypermetropia. Sources: https://www.allaboutvision.com/conditions/myopia/how-lenses-correct-nearsightedness/, https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physics/double-convex-lenses/which-type-of-lens-is-used-to-correct-myopia-and-which-type-is-used-to-correct-hypermetropia/

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.human_body.lens_concave_convex source.aao_concave_convex_lenses --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

> **Claim:** Under the 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline, normal is below 120/80 mm Hg; elevated is 120 to 129 systolic with diastolic below 80; stage 1 hypertension is 130 to 139 systolic or 80 to 89 diastolic; stage 2 is 140 or higher systolic or 90 or higher diastolic.

- **Concept:** Blood pressure categories and why it is checked (`concept.human_body.bloodpressure_categories`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L26 “Blood Pressure” · `card.human_body.026.c1` (text): 120 over 80. Two numbers, one heartbeat. / A blood pressure reading looks like a fraction, but it's really two moments in every heartbeat. What are those numbers measuring, and why do doctors bother checking?
  - L26 “Blood Pressure” · `card.human_body.026.c3` (comparison): The 2025 AHA/ACC guideline's four categories: Not high (Normal: systolic below 120 and diastolic below 80; Elevated: systolic 120 to 129, diastolic below 80) vs High (hypertension) (Stage 1: systolic 130 to 139, or diastolic 80 to 89; Stage 2: systolic 140 or higher, or diastolic 90 or higher)
- **Tested by:**
  - L26 `question.human_body.026.q1`: Under the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline, which of these readings counts as normal blood pressure? → **115/75 mm Hg**

## The number of alveoli in the human lung (American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, 2004) (American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine)

- **Source:** `source.ajrccm_ochs_alveoli_2004`
- **URL:** https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14512270/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.lung_alveoli_count`: unverified

> **Claim:** A 2004 study counted a mean of about 480 million alveoli in adult human lungs (range 274 to 790 million), with larger lungs having more.

- **Concept:** The alveoli, where gas is exchanged (`concept.human_body.lung_alveoli`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L32 “The Lungs” · `card.human_body.032.c1` (text): Your lungs are an upside-down tree with 480 million leaves. / Level 31's oxygen has to get from the air into your blood. The route runs down one trunk, out through thousands of branches, and ends in tiny air sacs with walls so thin that gas slips straight through.
  - L32 “The Lungs” · `card.human_body.032.c4` (fact): Your lungs hold about 480 million air sacs. / That's the average a 2004 study counted in adult lungs, and bigger lungs have more. Each sac is wrapped in tiny blood vessels called capillaries, and the barrier between air and blood is only about 0.5 micrometers thick. Oxygen passes through into the blood; carbon dioxide passes the other way.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Breathing” · `card.human_body.040.c3` (text): The round trip / Down the windpipe, out along the bronchial tree, through thousands of bronchioles to about 480 million air sacs. Oxygen crosses their thin walls into the blood and rides to your cells, where mitochondria use it to release energy from food. The exhaust, carbon dioxide, rides the blood back, crosses into the air sacs, and leaves as your diaphragm relaxes and your lungs spring back.
- **Tested by:**
  - L32 `question.human_body.032.q1`: About how many alveoli did a 2004 study count, on average, in adult human lungs? → **About 480 million**
  - L32 `question.human_body.032.q3`: Level 31's cells dump carbon dioxide into your blood. Where in your breathing system does it leave the blood? → **In the alveoli**
  - L38 `question.human_body.038.q3`: Emphysema damages the walls between air sacs. Why does that matter, given what Level 32 showed? → **Oxygen crosses into the blood there**
  - L40 `question.human_body.040.q3`: Breathing recap: which list follows a breath from the windpipe to where oxygen enters the blood? → **Windpipe, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Aarhus University research portal abstract and Kenhub: mean alveolar number 480 million, range 274 to 790 million, closely related to lung volume. Sources: https://pure.au.dk/portal/en/publications/the-number-of-alveoli-in-the-human-lung/, https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/alveoli

npm run verify:record -- fact.human_body.lung_alveoli_count source.ajrccm_ochs_alveoli_2004 --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.human_body.hayflick_carrel`: unverified

> **Claim:** Hayflick's finding overturned the claim, made by Alexis Carrel, that cells in culture could keep dividing forever; Hayflick linked the limit to aging.

- **Concept:** The Hayflick limit and telomeres (`concept.human_body.aging_division_limit`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L85 “Why We Age” · `card.human_body.085.c1` (text): Your cells can only divide so many times. / Scientists once believed cells grown in a dish could divide forever. In 1961 two researchers showed they can't, and that limit became one of the first clues to why bodies age.
  - L85 “Why We Age” · `card.human_body.085.c2` (text): The Hayflick limit / In 1961 Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead reported that normal human cells grown in a dish divide only about 40 to 60 times, then stop. - **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ScienceDirect Topics (Hayflick limit): the 1961 work refuted Alexis Carrel's contention that normal cells are immortal. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/hayflick-limit
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.human_body.telomere_shortening`: unverified

> **Claim:** Each chromosome ends in a telomere of repeated DNA; some repeats are cut off at every division until the telomeres are too short for the cell to divide successfully.

- **Concept:** The Hayflick limit and telomeres (`concept.human_body.aging_division_limit`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L85 “Why We Age” · `card.human_body.085.c3` (text): A fuse on every chromosome / Why the cap? Each chromosome ends in a telomere, a stretch of repeated DNA letters. Every time a cell divides, some of those repeats get cut off. Eventually the telomeres are too short for the cell to divide successfully. Remember Level 10's 330 billion cells replaced every day? Each division burns a little more fuse.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Growing and Changing” · `card.human_body.090.c2` (timeline): One life, from a single cell: Fertilization: Egg and sperm (23 chromosomes each) make a zygote with 46; Week 10 of pregnancy: The embryo is now a fetus; birth at about 40 weeks; About 8 to 14: Hypothalamus to pituitary to ovaries or testes: puberty begins; Mid-to-late 20s: The prefrontal cortex finishes maturing; Later life: Telomeres shorten and senescent cells build up
- **Tested by:**
  - L85 `question.human_body.085.q3`: Level 10 said about 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day. What does each of those divisions do to a cell's telomeres? → **Cuts off some of their repeats**
  - L90 `question.human_body.090.q4`: Growing and Changing recap, from Level 85: what happens to a chromosome's telomere each time the cell divides? → **Some of its repeats are cut off**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ScienceDirect Topics (Hayflick limit): telomere shortening at each division is the primary mechanism behind the limit, triggering growth arrest when telomeres are critically short. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/hayflick-limit
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

npm run verify:record -- fact.human_body.telomere_shortening source.asu_embryo_hayflick_limit --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"

## Oxygen at high altitude (BMJ, 1998) (BMJ)

- **Source:** `source.bmj_peacock_altitude_1998`
- **URL:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114067/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.altitude_acclimatization_changes`: unverified

> **Claim:** The body acclimatizes to altitude by breathing more deeply and faster, raising heart rate, and over time making more red blood cells to carry oxygen.

- **Concept:** How bodies adapt to altitude (`concept.human_body.altitude_acclimatization`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L36 “Breathing at Altitude” · `card.human_body.036.c3` (text): The body turns up the supply / Stay high for a while and your body adapts, a process called acclimatization. You breathe more deeply and faster, your heart beats faster, and over time you make more red blood cells to carry oxygen. It's the body's version of hiring extra delivery drivers when every shipment arrives short.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.memory_hm_minutes`: unverified

> **Claim:** Molaison kept memories from before the surgery, such as scenes from his childhood, but minutes after meeting someone he had no recollection of the meeting.

- **Concept:** The hippocampus and new memories (`concept.human_body.memory_hippocampus`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L56 “Memory” · `card.human_body.056.c1` (text): In 1953, one surgery stopped a man making new memories. / Henry Molaison was 27 when surgeons operated to control his severe seizures. Afterward, he could meet you and chat, and minutes after you left the room, have no memory of the meeting. His loss showed science where new memories are made.
  - L56 “Memory” · `card.human_body.056.c2` (text): The library was fine. The librarian was gone. / Surgeons had removed tissue from each side of his brain, including much of the hippocampus. That small structure deep in the brain acts as a memory indexer: it sends new memories to the right part of the cerebrum for long-term storage and fetches them back. Molaison kept memories from before surgery, like scenes from his childhood. He just couldn't file new ones.
- **Tested by:**
  - L56 `question.human_body.056.q1`: After his 1953 surgery, what could Henry Molaison no longer do? → **Form new long-term memories**
  - L56 `question.human_body.056.q3`: Level 54 said the temporal lobes help form memories. Which deep structure did Molaison's case show files new memories? → **The hippocampus**
  - L57 `question.human_body.057.q3`: Level 56 showed the hippocampus filing new memories. Which sleep does storing memories most likely need? → **Both non-REM and REM sleep**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. MedLink notes his short-term memory and older memories were intact while new long-term memories were lost. Sources: https://www.medlink.com/news/neurology-through-history-what-patient-h-m-taught-us-about-the-secrets-of-the-hippocampus

  - L26 “Blood Pressure” · `card.human_body.026.c2` (text): Push, then pause / Blood pressure is the force of blood pushing against the walls of your arteries. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.capillary_exchange`: unverified

> **Claim:** Capillary walls are a single thin layer of cells, and through them oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between the blood and the tissues.

- **Concept:** Capillaries, where delivery happens (`concept.human_body.vessel_capillaries`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L23 “Blood Vessels” · `card.human_body.023.c2` (comparison): Three kinds of road: Arteries (Carry blood away from the heart; Thick walls; the big ones stretch with each push, then recoil) vs Veins (Carry blood back to the heart; Lower pressure, thinner walls; Many, especially in the limbs, have one-way valves) vs Capillaries (Link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins; Walls just one thin layer of cells)
  - L23 “Blood Vessels” · `card.human_body.023.c4` (text): Capillaries: where the delivery happens / Arteries and veins are only roads. The drop-off happens in capillaries, vessels so narrow (about 8 to 10 micrometers) that red blood cells squeeze through in single file. Their walls are a single thin layer of cells, so oxygen and nutrients cross out to your tissues and wastes cross in. All the pumping from Level 21 exists to get blood to this doorstep.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Heart and Blood” · `card.human_body.030.c2` (text): One lap, two circuits / Start in the left ventricle. One push sends your red cell out along an artery, branching smaller and smaller until it squeezes single file through a capillary and hands its oxygen to the tissues. Now a duskier red, it drifts home through the veins, with valves keeping it on course, into the right atrium. The right ventricle sends it to the lungs to reload, and it returns to the left side bright red again. One lap, two trips through the heart.
- **Tested by:**
  - L23 `question.human_body.023.q2`: Why do oxygen and nutrients leave the blood in capillaries, not in arteries? → **Capillary walls are one thin layer of cells**
  - L27 `question.human_body.027.q3`: Harvey couldn't see how blood crossed from arteries into veins. What did Malpighi's microscope reveal in 1661? → **Capillaries linking small arteries to small veins**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. SEER training module: capillary walls are a single layer of endothelial cells, where nutrients, oxygen and wastes are exchanged with the tissues. Sources: https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/blood/classification.html
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

  - L56 “Memory” · `card.human_body.056.c4` (text): Why you forget, and how to fight back / In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus published results from testing his own memory with nonsense syllables. It's one of the most replicated findings in psychology. Little and often wins.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Murre and Dros (2015) replicated the curve, showing steep early loss that levels off; Britannica dates Uber das Gedachtnis to 1885. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.leeuwenhoek_bacteria`: unverified

> **Claim:** Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria; in 1683 he described "little animalcules" in the plaque from his own teeth.

- **Concept:** Microscopes and cell theory (`concept.human_body.microscopes_cells`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L9 “How We Learned About the Body” · `card.human_body.009.c3` (timeline): Looking closer, then smaller: 1543: Vesalius's book maps the body from human dissection; 1665: Robert Hooke names 'cells' after the boxes he sees in cork; 1683: Leeuwenhoek describes bacteria from his own teeth; Late 1830s: Schleiden and Schwann: all living things are made of cells
  - L9 “How We Learned About the Body” · `card.human_body.009.c4` (text): Microbiology began with a set of teeth / Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own single lenses, magnifying up to about 300 times. In 1683 he looked at the plaque from his own teeth and saw 'little animalcules' moving about: bacteria, seen for the first time. The microbes you met in Level 8 had been living on people all along. It took a homemade lens to notice them.
  - L42 “Teeth” · `card.human_body.042.c4` (text): Hard, but not alive / Enamel is the hardest substance in your body, about 95 percent mineral by weight, mostly crystals of calcium phosphate. But once formed, it holds no living cells: the cells that built it are lost when the tooth comes in. So unlike bone, enamel can't remodel or regrow. It's also prime real estate. Level 9's Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria in the plaque from his own teeth.
  - L72 “Germs” · `card.human_body.072.c3` (text): The germ that slipped through the filter / Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria back in Level 9. Viruses were far too small for his lens. In 1892, Dmitry Ivanovsky found that a disease of tobacco plants passed through a filter fine enough to trap bacteria, so something smaller was carrying it. Most viruses measure from about 20 to a few hundred nanometers, and none can multiply outside a living cell. A virus is a set of instructions looking for a factory.
  - L97 “Surgery Then and Now” · `card.human_body.097.c3` (text): Surviving the operation, not the wound / Painless surgery still had a killer problem. In Joseph Lister's ward in Glasgow, 45 to 50 percent of amputation patients died of sepsis, an infection, between 1861 and 1865. After reading Louis Pasteur's germ theory, Lister concluded that microorganisms caused it, the same kind of tiny life Leeuwenhoek first spotted in Level 9. From 1865 he cleaned instruments and wounds with carbolic acid, and deaths in his ward fell sharply.
- **Tested by:**
  - L9 `question.human_body.009.q3`: Level 8's resident bacteria went unseen for most of history. Who first saw bacteria, and where? → **Leeuwenhoek, in plaque from his own teeth**
  - L10 `question.human_body.010.q5`: Building Blocks recap, from Level 9: what did Robert Hooke name after looking at cork through a lens? → **The cell**
  - L42 `question.human_body.042.q3`: Level 9's Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria. Where did he find them? → **In plaque from his own teeth**
  - L72 `question.human_body.072.q3`: Leeuwenhoek's lens revealed bacteria in Level 9. What 1892 finding showed viruses are smaller still? → **A tobacco disease that passed through a bacteria-trapping filter**
  - L97 `question.human_body.097.q3`: Level 9 met the first person to see bacteria. How does Leeuwenhoek's discovery connect to Lister's surgery? → **Lister fought the kind of microbes Leeuwenhoek first saw**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Royal Society and PMC histories: his 17 September 1683 letter described moving animalcules in plaque from his own teeth, the first undisputed description of bacteria. Sources: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10756362/, https://www.britannica.com/biography/Antonie-van-Leeuwenhoek

### ☐ `fact.human_body.capillary_link`: unverified

> **Claim:** Capillaries are the tiny vessels that link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins.

- **Concept:** Capillaries, where delivery happens (`concept.human_body.vessel_capillaries`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L23 “Blood Vessels” · `card.human_body.023.c2` (comparison): Three kinds of road: Arteries (Carry blood away from the heart; Thick walls; the big ones stretch with each push, then recoil) vs Veins (Carry blood back to the heart; Lower pressure, thinner walls; Many, especially in the limbs, have one-way valves) vs Capillaries (Link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins; Walls just one thin layer of cells)
  - L23 “Blood Vessels” · `card.human_body.023.c4` (text): Capillaries: where the delivery happens / Arteries and veins are only roads. The drop-off happens in capillaries, vessels so narrow (about 8 to 10 micrometers) that red blood cells squeeze through in single file. Their walls are a single thin layer of cells, so oxygen and nutrients cross out to your tissues and wastes cross in. All the pumping from Level 21 exists to get blood to this doorstep.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Heart and Blood” · `card.human_body.030.c2` (text): One lap, two circuits / Start in the left ventricle. One push sends your red cell out along an artery, branching smaller and smaller until it squeezes single file through a capillary and hands its oxygen to the tissues. Now a duskier red, it drifts home through the veins, with valves keeping it on course, into the right atrium. The right ventricle sends it to the lungs to reload, and it returns to the left side bright red again. One lap, two trips through the heart.
- **Tested by:**

  - L27 `question.human_body.027.q3`: Harvey couldn't see how blood crossed from arteries into veins. What did Malpighi's microscope reveal in 1661? → **Capillaries linking small arteries to small veins**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica Harvey article: capillaries are small vessels linking the arteries and veins. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/biography/William-Harvey/Key-discoveries-and-influences

### ☐ `fact.human_body.muscle_pull_only`: unverified

> **Claim:** Muscles can only contract, so they pull and never push; they work in opposing (antagonistic) pairs, and when one contracts, its partner relaxes.

- **Concept:** Muscles only pull, so they work in pairs (`concept.human_body.muscle_pull_pairs`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L16 “How Muscles Pull” · `card.human_body.016.c1` (text): Your muscles can't push. So how do you push a door? / Every muscle in your body can only pull. Yet you push doors, shopping carts and elevator buttons all day. The answer is teamwork, and it starts deep inside each muscle fiber.
  - L16 “How Muscles Pull” · `card.human_body.016.c3` (text): Pull only, so muscles come in pairs / Sliding filaments can shorten a muscle, but a muscle can only contract, never push. So muscles work in pairs that pull in opposite directions. Your biceps pulls to bend your elbow; your triceps, on the back of your arm, pulls to straighten it. At the knee, the quadriceps straighten and the hamstrings bend. When one partner pulls, the other relaxes.
  - L16 “How Muscles Pull” · `card.human_body.016.c4` (text): Every push is a pull in disguise / So how do you push that door? Your triceps pulls to straighten your elbow, and your arm drives forward while the biceps relaxes. No muscle pushed anything. Every push you'll ever make is a pull happening somewhere else.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: Bones and Muscles” · `card.human_body.020.c4` (text): One sip, the whole chapter / Lift that cup. Your nervous system signals the biceps, skeletal muscle you control. Myosin pulls actin, the muscle shortens, and a tendon carries the pull to your forearm bone. The elbow, a hinge joint where ligaments connect the bones, bends. The triceps relaxes, ready to pull back the other way.
- **Tested by:**
  - L16 `question.human_body.016.q2`: Why do skeletal muscles work in pairs on opposite sides of a joint? → **A muscle only pulls, so a partner pulls back**
  - L16 `question.human_body.016.q3`: Level 13 called the elbow a hinge joint. Which muscle pulls to straighten it? → **The triceps**
  - L17 `question.human_body.017.q3`: Level 16's biceps pulls to bend the elbow. What carries that pull from the muscle to the bone? → **A tendon**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. CK-12: muscles pull but cannot push, so they work in antagonistic pairs such as biceps and triceps; OpenStax 11.1: muscles are arranged in pairs based on their functions. Layer four is ours. Soap and water scrub germs away, vaccines train memory in advance, and penicillin blocks bacteria from building their cell walls.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.health_trial_blinding`: unverified

> **Claim:** In a blind test, patients don't know whether they got the real drug or a placebo; in a double-blind test, neither the patients nor their doctors know.

- **Appears in:**
  - L96 “Testing Medicines” · `card.human_body.096.c4` (text): Random and blind / Back to 1948's envelopes. Allocating patients at random stops researchers from choosing, even unconsciously, who gets the new drug, a choice that could tilt the result. Blinding goes further. In a blind test, patients don't know whether they got the drug or the placebo; in a double-blind test, their doctors don't know either. Nobody's hopes get a vote.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.altitude_acclimatization_changes`: unverified

> **Claim:** The body acclimatizes to altitude by breathing more deeply and faster, raising heart rate, and over time making more red blood cells to carry oxygen.

- **Concept:** How bodies adapt to altitude (`concept.human_body.altitude_acclimatization`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L36 “Breathing at Altitude” · `card.human_body.036.c3` (text): The body turns up the supply / Stay high for a while and your body adapts, a process called acclimatization. You breathe more deeply and faster, your heart beats faster, and over time you make more red blood cells to carry oxygen. It's the body's version of hiring extra delivery drivers when every shipment arrives short.
- **Tested by:**
  - L36 `question.human_body.036.q2`: After days at high altitude, how has the body adjusted to the thinner air? → **Deeper breathing and more red blood cells**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica and Peacock (BMJ) corroborate each other: increased ventilation and heart rate, and hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin so red cell production rises. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114067/

### ☐ `fact.human_body.altitude_same_percent`: unverified

> **Claim:** The share of oxygen in air stays about 21 percent at every altitude, but air pressure falls with height, so each breath brings less oxygen into the lungs.

- **Concept:** Why air is thinner up high (`concept.human_body.altitude_thin_air`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L36 “Breathing at Altitude” · `card.human_body.036.c1` (text): In 1978, two climbers reached the top of Everest on the mountain's own air. / Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler were the first to climb Everest without bottled oxygen. Up there, the air is still about 21 percent oxygen, the same share as at the beach. So why is breathing on a mountaintop so hard?
  - L36 “Breathing at Altitude” · `card.human_body.036.c2` (text): Same recipe, thinner air / The mix never changes; the pressure does. The higher you go, the lower the air pressure, so every breath brings less oxygen into your lungs even though the percentage is the same. At the height of Everest's summit, air pressure is only about 30 percent of its sea-level value. Same gulp, much less oxygen inside it.
- **Tested by:**
  - L36 `question.human_body.036.q1`: High on a mountain, what happens to the share of oxygen in the air? → **It stays the same; the pressure drops**

  - L40 `question.human_body.040.q4`: Breathing recap, from Level 36: at the height of Everest's summit, air pressure is about what share of its sea-level value? → **About 30 percent**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Peacock (BMJ: percentage of oxygen constant while pressure falls) and Britannica (lower barometric pressure lowers alveolar oxygen pressure) corroborate each other. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1114067/

### ☐ `fact.human_body.eye_blind_spot`: unverified

> **Claim:** Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, a patch with no rods or cones; we rarely notice it because the two eyes' views overlap and the brain fills in or ignores the gap.

- **Appears in:**
  - L62 “How Eyes See” · `card.human_body.062.c4` (fact): Each of your eyes has a blind spot, and you're not seeing it right now. / It sits where the optic nerve leaves the retina, a patch with no rods or cones, so nothing landing there is detected. You don't notice the hole because your two eyes' views overlap, and even with one eye shut your brain fills in or ignores the gap. Your brain isn't just receiving the picture. It's quietly editing it.
  - L69 “Optical Illusions” · `card.human_body.069.c4` (text): You've been edited all along / You've met this editor before. In Level 62 your brain turned the upside-down image on your retina upright, and quietly filled in each eye's blind spot. Illusions aren't a glitch in an otherwise perfect camera. They're the rare moments you catch your brain at work.

A convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and pulls the focus forward, which helps farsighted eyes. A contact lens does the same job as a thin lens worn right on the surface of your eye.

## Hyperopia (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

- **Source:** `source.britannica_hyperopia`
- **URL:** https://www.britannica.com/science/hyperopia
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.lens_concave_convex`: unverified

> **Claim:** A concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads light rays apart and corrects nearsightedness; a convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and corrects farsightedness.

- **Concept:** How glasses and contacts fix focus (`concept.human_body.senses_corrective_lenses`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L64 “Glasses and Contacts” · `card.human_body.064.c1` (text): Raphael painted a pope holding a lens that curves inward. / In the portrait, from the late 1510s, Pope Leo X holds a concave lens: he was nearsighted. It's an early picture of a lens for blurry distance vision, and today's glasses still work on the same idea. To see why, start with what goes wrong inside the eye.
  - L64 “Glasses and Contacts” · `card.human_body.064.c3` (text): Bend it back / A lens in front of your eye moves the focus. A concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads light rays apart, pushing the focus back onto the retina: the fix for nearsightedness. A convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and pulls the focus forward, which helps farsighted eyes. A contact lens does the same job as a thin lens worn right on the surface of your eye.
- **Tested by:**
  - L64 `question.human_body.064.q2`: Why does a concave lens help a nearsighted eye see far away? → **It spreads rays so the focus moves back**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. All About Vision: a concave lens is thinner at the center and diverges light so it focuses further back, on the retina; CK-12: a convex lens converges light rays to correct hypermetropia. Sources: https://www.allaboutvision.com/conditions/myopia/how-lenses-correct-nearsightedness/, https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physics/double-convex-lenses/which-type-of-lens-is-used-to-correct-myopia-and-which-type-is-used-to-correct-hypermetropia/

### ☐ `fact.human_body.illusion_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts objective reality; illusions can come from light or poor lighting, from the eye itself, and from how the brain processes visual information.

- **Appears in:**
  - L69 “Optical Illusions” · `card.human_body.069.c2` (text): Seeing isn't measuring / An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality. Some illusions come from light or poor lighting, some from the eye itself, and many from how your brain processes what the eyes send. The two lines are the Müller-Lyer illusion, published in 1889 by Franz Carl Müller-Lyer: equal lines, but the one with fins flaring outward looks longer. What you see is your brain's reading of the scene, not a ruler's.
- **Tested by:**
  - L69 `question.human_body.069.q1`: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, which of two equal lines looks longer? → **The one with fins flaring outward**

EBSCO Research Starters (Muller-Lyer illusion): the illusion plays on differences in people's visual systems, showing perception depends on how the brain interprets visual data; the Illusions Index describes the visual system deceived by context. Sources: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/muller-lyer-illusion/, https://www.illusionsindex.org/i/mueller-lyer/

## Why is the visual image projected on the retina of the human eye upside down? (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

- **Source:** `source.britannica_retina_image_inverted`
- **URL:** https://www.britannica.com/science/Why-is-the-visual-image-projected-on-the-retina-of-the-human-eye-upside-down
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.eye_image_inverted`: unverified

> **Claim:** The cornea and lens together act like a convex lens, so the image formed on the retina is upside down; the brain corrects for this, and we see the world upright.

- **Concept:** From retina to brain (`concept.human_body.senses_retina_to_brain`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L62 “How Eyes See” · `card.human_body.062.c1` (text): Your eye takes every picture upside down. You've never noticed. / The image that lands at the back of your eye is inverted, yet the world looks the right way up. Follow a beam of light through your eye to find out who does the fixing.
  - L62 “How Eyes See” · `card.human_body.062.c3` (text): The brain develops the picture / In the retina, special cells called photoreceptors turn light into electrical signals. The optic nerve carries those signals to your brain, which turns them into the images you see. Because the cornea and lens together act like one convex lens, the image on the retina is upside down, and your brain corrects for it. Your eye collects the light. Your brain does the seeing.
  - L69 “Optical Illusions” · `card.human_body.069.c4` (text): You've been edited all along / You've met this editor before. In Level 62 your brain turned the upside-down image on your retina upright, and quietly filled in each eye's blind spot. Illusions aren't a glitch in an otherwise perfect camera. They're the rare moments you catch your brain at work.
- **Tested by:**
  - L62 `question.human_body.062.q3`: Level 4 defined a tissue as similar cells working together. What do the special cells in your retina's tissue do? → **Turn light into electrical signals**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Scientific American ('Right Side Up', 2008): "The lens in your eye casts an upside-down image on your retina, but you see the world upright." Sources: https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/right-side-up-2008-05/

- **Source:** `source.hekint_lind_scurvy`

### ☐ `fact.human_body.lind_own_theory`: unverified

> **Claim:** Lind did not see scurvy as a deficiency disease: he blamed it mainly on damp air and a coarse diet the body failed to digest, and his 1753 Treatise did not clearly declare citrus the cure.

- **Concept:** James Lind's scurvy trial (`concept.human_body.scurvy_lind_trial`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L49 “Vitamins and Scurvy” · `card.human_body.049.c3` (timeline): Twelve sailors, then decades: May 1747: On HMS Salisbury, James Lind gives 12 sailors with scurvy six remedies, two men each; Days later: The pair given oranges and lemons recover fastest; one is fit for duty within about six days; 1753: Lind's Treatise of the Scurvy reports the trial, without naming citrus the cure; 1795: The Royal Navy makes lemon juice standard issue; 1932: Vitamin C is identified as the factor that prevents scurvy
  - L49 “Vitamins and Scurvy” · `card.human_body.049.c4` (text): Why the lesson took 48 years / Lind's comparison is seen as an early controlled clinical trial, but he didn't draw the lesson we see in it. He blamed scurvy mainly on damp air and a coarse diet the body failed to digest, not on a missing nutrient. He later recommended rob, a juice concentrate made by heating, and heat destroys vitamin C. The Admiralty adopted lemon juice in 1795, persuaded by Gilbert Blane. The evidence came early; the explanation came much later.
- **Tested by:**
  - L49 `question.human_body.049.q2`: James Lind saw citrus work in 1747. Why didn't he present it as the cure for scurvy? → **He saw scurvy mainly as a problem of damp air and digestion**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Hektoen International quotes Lind blaming moisture and a gross, poorly digested diet; Bartholomew (2002) says he saw scurvy as faulty digestion and did not declare citrus the definitive cure. Sources: https://hekint.org/2017/01/29/the-mysteries-of-james-lind-and-scurvy/, https://academic.oup.com/pmj/article-abstract/78/925/695/7045929

## Adelson's Checker-Shadow Illusion (The Illusions Index)

- **Source:** `source.illusionsindex_checker_shadow`
- **URL:** https://www.illusionsindex.org/i/adelson-s-checker-shadow-illusion
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.checker_shadow_1995`: unverified

> **Claim:** In Edward Adelson's 1995 checker-shadow illusion, a square in a cylinder's shadow looks much lighter than a square outside it, although both are exactly the same shade of grey.

- **Concept:** Correcting for shadows (`concept.human_body.senses_lightness_constancy`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L69 “Optical Illusions” · `card.human_body.069.c3` (text): The shadow that fools you / In Edward Adelson's 1995 checker-shadow illusion, a cylinder casts a shadow across a checkerboard. A square inside the shadow looks much lighter than one outside it, yet they're the exact same grey. Your visual system estimates where the light comes from and judges each surface's own shade, correcting for shadow. On a flat picture that correction misleads you. In the real world, it keeps a white shirt looking white in the shade.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: The Senses” · `card.human_body.070.c3` (text): Sensing isn't perceiving / Sensation is a receptor detecting something. Perception is your brain organizing and interpreting it into an experience. They aren't the same: Level 69's checkerboard sent your eyes two identical greys, and your brain perceived two different ones. Your receptors collect the data. Your brain writes the story.
- **Tested by:**
  - L69 `question.human_body.069.q2`: In Adelson's checker-shadow illusion, why does the square in the shadow look lighter than it really is? → **The brain corrects for a shadow it thinks is there**
  - L70 `question.human_body.070.q3`: Senses recap: Adelson's two squares send your eyes the same grey but look different. Where does the difference arise? → **In perception: the brain interprets the same input differently**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Michael Bach (Optical Illusions): Ted Adelson published the illusion in 1995; square B appears brighter, but isolated, the two squares have identical luminance. Sources: https://michaelbach.de/ot/lum-adelsonCheckShadow/
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

```

## Muller-Lyer Illusion (The Illusions Index)

- **Source:** `source.illusionsindex_muller_lyer`
- **URL:** https://www.illusionsindex.org/i/mueller-lyer/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.muller_lyer_1889`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the Muller-Lyer illusion, published by Franz Carl Muller-Lyer in 1889, two lines of equal length look different: the one with fins flaring outward at its ends looks longer than the one capped with arrowheads.

- **Concept:** Optical illusions (`concept.human_body.senses_illusions`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L69 “Optical Illusions” · `card.human_body.069.c1` (text): Two lines, exactly the same length. One looks longer. / Add arrowheads to one line and outward-flaring fins to the other, and the fins win. Your eyes aren't broken. Your brain is interpreting what it sees, and here the interpretation goes wrong.
  - L69 “Optical Illusions” · `card.human_body.069.c2` (text): Seeing isn't measuring / An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts reality. Some illusions come from light or poor lighting, some from the eye itself, and many from how your brain processes what the eyes send. The two lines are the Müller-Lyer illusion, published in 1889 by Franz Carl Müller-Lyer: equal lines, but the one with fins flaring outward looks longer. What you see is your brain's reading of the scene, not a ruler's.
- **Tested by:**
  - L69 `question.human_body.069.q1`: In the Müller-Lyer illusion, which of two equal lines looks longer? → **The one with fins flaring outward**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. EBSCO Research Starters: Franz Carl Muller-Lyer devised the illusion in 1889; two lines of the same length look different because of the arrows at their ends, one set pointing outward and one inward. Sources: https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/muller-lyer-illusion/
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

In 2009, a team finally did the counting, and the answer came out smaller. Then comes the better question: how does each one of those cells pass a message on?
  - L52 “Neurons” · `card.human_body.052.c2` (fact): Your brain has about 86 billion neurons. / Frederico Azevedo and colleagues dissolved brain tissue into an even soup of loose cell nuclei, stained and counted the nuclei in samples, then scaled up. Across four men's brains, the average was about 86 billion neurons, with about 85 billion other cells alongside them. Not quite 100 billion, but nobody's complaining.
  - L54 “Parts of the Brain” · `card.human_body.054.c4` (fact): The 'little brain' holds about 80 percent of your neurons. / The cerebral cortex is about 82 percent of the brain's mass but holds about 16 billion of its roughly 86 billion neurons. The cerebellum, about 10 percent of the mass, packs in about 69 billion. Remember Level 3? Red blood cells won the headcount while muscle won the mass. Same lesson: size isn't headcount.
- **Tested by:**
  - L52 `question.human_body.052.q1`: About how many neurons did Azevedo's team count in an adult human brain? → **About 86 billion**
  - L54 `question.human_body.054.q3`: Level 52 counted about 86 billion neurons. Which part of the brain holds roughly 80 percent of them? → **The cerebellum**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. A 2025 PMC review and Herculano-Houzel (2009) report the 86.1 billion neuron average from four male brains and about 85 billion non-neuronal cells. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11884752/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2776484/

## Why the 1948 MRC trial of streptomycin used treatment allocation based on random numbers (The James Lind Library)

- **Source:** `source.jll_streptomycin_randomization`
- **URL:** https://www.jameslindlibrary.org/articles/why-the-1948-mrc-trial-of-streptomycin-used-treatment-allocation-based-on-random-numbers/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.human_body.health_trial_random_bias`: unverified

> **Claim:** Random allocation stops investigators from choosing, consciously or unconsciously, which patients get the new treatment, which could bias the result.

- **Concept:** Placebos, randomization and blinding (`concept.human_body.health_placebo_control`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L96 “Testing Medicines” · `card.human_body.096.c4` (text): Random and blind / Back to 1948's envelopes. Allocating patients at random stops researchers from choosing, even unconsciously, who gets the new drug, a choice that could tilt the result. Blinding goes further. In a blind test, patients don't know whether they got the drug or the placebo; in a double-blind test, their doctors don't know either. Nobody's hopes get a vote.
- **Tested by:**
  - L100 `question.human_body.100.q9`: Mastery: which kind of trial showed that sugar doesn't make kids hyper? → **Double-blind trials, where no one knew who had sugar**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. James Lind Library: random allocation removes the 'conscious or unconscious temptation to allow biased allocation'; ACS: phase 3 participants are often picked at random. Sources: https://www.cancer.org/cancer/managing-cancer/making-treatment-decisions/clinical-trials/what-you-need-to-know/phases-of-clinical-trials.html
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.human_body.adaptive_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** Acquired (adaptive) immunity develops with exposure to antigens: the immune system builds a defense against each specific antigen it meets.

- **Appears in:**
  - L73 “The Immune System” · `card.human_body.073.c4` (text): Specialists who learn and remember / Your second defense, acquired immunity, develops as you meet germs. It relies on lymphocytes, white blood cells of two kinds. B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies: proteins that lock onto one specific antigen, usually a protein on a germ's surface, and make it easier to destroy. T cells attack directly and help run the response. Afterwards, some B and T cells stay on as memory, so the next time that germ turns up, the answer comes faster.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.health_placebo_compare`: unverified

> **Claim:** In randomized controlled trials, comparing a group given the treatment with a group given a placebo shows whether changes come from the treatment or occur by chance.

- **Appears in:**
  - L96 “Testing Medicines” · `card.human_body.096.c3` (text): The fake pill that keeps trials honest / In many trials, one group gets the medicine and another gets a placebo: an inactive substance that looks just like it. Why? People can feel better simply because they expect a treatment to help. That's the placebo effect. Comparing the two groups shows whether changes come from the treatment or from chance. If the pill and the placebo do equally well, the pill isn't the one doing the work.
- **Tested by:**
  - L96 `question.human_body.096.q2`: Why do many clinical trials give one group an inactive placebo instead of nothing at all? → **To separate the drug's real effect from expectation and chance**

  - L99 `question.human_body.099.q3`: In the 1994 sugar study every boy got a placebo. Using Level 96, what does the mothers' reaction show? → **Expectation changed what they saw**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NCCIH: 'comparing results from the two groups suggests whether changes in the test group result from the treatment or occur by chance.' Britannica describes placebo-controlled testing. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/placebo

### ☐ `fact.human_body.dna_46_chromosomes`: unverified

> **Claim:** Human DNA is packaged into 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs.

- **Concept:** Where the body keeps DNA (`concept.human_body.dna_location`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L5 “DNA, the Instruction Book” · `card.human_body.005.c3` (text): Kept in the command center / Nearly every cell in your body has the same DNA. Most of it sits in the nucleus, Level 2's command center, packaged into 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Its two strands twist into a double helix, a spiral ladder whose rungs are paired letters: A with T, C with G. A small amount of DNA also lives in the mitochondria, the cell's power stations.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: The Building Blocks” · `card.human_body.010.c2` (text): Zoom from you to a single gene / Start with you: 11 organ systems. Zoom into the digestive system and pick one organ, the stomach, built from four tissue types. Zoom into a tissue: similar cells working together, part of about 30 trillion human cells. Open one cell and find the nucleus, holding 46 chromosomes of DNA. Read one gene, and a ribosome builds a protein from its message.
  - L81 “From One Cell to a Baby” · `card.human_body.081.c2` (text): Half a set from each side / It begins with fertilization: a sperm cell and an egg cell fuse into one new cell, the zygote. Each of those two cells carries exactly 23 chromosomes, one of each pair. Together they make 46. Remember Level 5's 23 pairs? This is where they come from: in every pair, one chromosome is from each parent.
  - L82 “Inherited Traits” · `card.human_body.082.c2` (text): Two copies of almost everything / Your 46 chromosomes come as 23 pairs, so wherever DNA varies between people, you carry two versions, called alleles: one from each parent. For some traits, one allele is dominant: a single copy is enough to show, and it masks the other, recessive one. Genes come in pairs, like shoes, one from each parent's closet.
- **Tested by:**
  - L63 `question.human_body.063.q3`: Level 5 packed your DNA into chromosomes. Why is red-green color blindness far more common in men? → **Its genes are on the X, and men have one X**
  - L81 `question.human_body.081.q3`: Level 5 said nearly every cell in your body has the same DNA. How does one zygote still produce nerve, muscle and liver cells? → **Its dividing cells specialize while keeping the same DNA**
  - L98 `question.human_body.098.q3`: Level 5 showed nearly every cell in one body carries the same DNA. Why could Ronald Herrick's kidney join Richard's body without rejection? → **Identical twins are genetically identical, so their antigens match**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. MedlinePlus Genetics: each cell normally contains 23 pairs of chromosomes, for a total of 46. Sources: https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/understanding/basics/howmanychromosomes/
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.human_body.cell_mitochondria`: unverified

> **Claim:** Mitochondria convert energy from food into a form the cell can use; they generate most of the chemical energy that powers the cell.

- **Concept:** The main parts of a cell (`concept.human_body.cell_parts`)
- **Appears in:**

It sends out directions telling the cell when to grow, mature, divide or die. Out in the cytoplasm, mitochondria are the power stations: they turn energy from food into a form the cell can use. Orders from the hall, power from the stations: that's a working town.
  - L5 “DNA, the Instruction Book” · `card.human_body.005.c3` (text): Kept in the command center / Nearly every cell in your body has the same DNA. Most of it sits in the nucleus, Level 2's command center, packaged into 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Its two strands twist into a double helix, a spiral ladder whose rungs are paired letters: A with T, C with G. A small amount of DNA also lives in the mitochondria, the cell's power stations.
  - L18 “Getting Stronger” · `card.human_body.018.c3` (text): Endurance builds the power supply / Long, steady exercise changes muscle in a different way. More engines, more fuel lines.
  - L31 “Why We Breathe” · `card.human_body.031.c2` (text): Your cells burn food with oxygen / Remember Level 2's mitochondria, the cell's power stations? This is what they need your breath for.   - L50 “Milestone: Fuel and Oxygen” · `card.human_body.050.c2` (text): From lunch to a power station / Digestion breaks the starch in your lunch into simple sugars, and your body turns them into glucose, your cells' main fuel. The small intestine absorbs it, and your blood takes it to the liver first, then on to cells all over your body. Inside each cell, Level 2's mitochondria convert the energy from food into a form the cell can use. Fuel you don't need right away can be stored in the liver, muscles and body fat.
  - L50 “Milestone: Fuel and Oxygen” · `card.human_body.050.c3` (text): Fuel meets oxygen / Mitochondria can't release that energy from fuel alone. In cellular respiration, cells combine oxygen with food molecules to free their chemical energy. Breakfast and breath end up in the same tiny place.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.breathing_cells_oxygen_co2`: unverified

### ☐ `fact.human_body.breathing_cells_oxygen_co2`: unverified

> **Claim:** Cells need oxygen to make the body's energy; the carbon dioxide they make passes into the blood, which must get rid of it, and in the lungs it moves from the blood into the air sacs to be breathed out.

- **Concept:** Why cells need oxygen (`concept.human_body.breathing_cell_respiration`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L31 “Why We Breathe” · `card.human_body.031.c3` (text): Breathing out is taking out the trash / Carbon dioxide can't pile up inside you. It passes from your cells into your blood, which has to get rid of it. In your lungs it crosses from the blood into the air, and your next breath out carries it away. So every breath is a two-way trip: oxygen in for your cells, their exhaust out.
  - L40 “Checkpoint: Breathing” · `card.human_body.040.c3` (text): The round trip / Down the windpipe, out along the bronchial tree, through thousands of bronchioles to about 480 million air sacs. Oxygen crosses their thin walls into the blood and rides to your cells, where mitochondria use it to release energy from food. The exhaust, carbon dioxide, rides the blood back, crosses into the air sacs, and leaves as your diaphragm relaxes and your lungs spring back.
- **Tested by:**
  - L32 `question.human_body.032.q3`: Level 31's cells dump carbon dioxide into your blood. Where in your breathing system does it leave the blood? → **In the alveoli**
  - L37 `question.human_body.037.q3`: Level 31's cells keep giving off carbon dioxide. What happens to it while you hold your breath? → **It builds up and sets off your breathing alarm**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica: cellular respiration combines oxygen with food and discards carbon dioxide as waste; OpenStax 22.1: gases cross the respiratory membrane between alveoli and blood by diffusion. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/cellular-respiration, https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/22-1-organs-and-structures-of-the-respiratory-system, https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits

So before a transplant, doctors check blood type and tissue type in donor and recipient; the closer the match, the lower the risk of rejection. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.fertilization_egg_sperm`: unverified

> **Claim:** Development begins at fertilization, when a sperm cell and an egg cell fuse into a single new cell called the zygote.

- **Concept:** Fertilization: egg and sperm make one cell (`concept.human_body.fertilization_zygote`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L81 “From One Cell to a Baby” · `card.human_body.081.c1` (text): Every person you've ever met started as one cell. / So did you. That first cell had no heart, no brain and no bones, just a full set of instructions. About 40 weeks later, there was a baby. Here's how one cell pulls that off.
  - L81 “From One Cell to a Baby” · `card.human_body.081.c2` (text): Half a set from each side / It begins with fertilization: a sperm cell and an egg cell fuse into one new cell, the zygote. Each of those two cells carries exactly 23 chromosomes, one of each pair. Together they make 46. Remember Level 5's 23 pairs? This is where they come from: in every pair, one chromosome is from each parent.

- **Tested by:**
  - L81 `question.human_body.081.q1`: At fertilization, how many chromosomes does each egg or sperm cell carry? → **23**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica (zygote): the zygote is the cell formed by the union of egg and sperm; ACOG describes fertilization of the egg by a sperm. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/science/zygote, https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/how-your-fetus-grows-during-pregnancy

### ☐ `fact.human_body.hair_cells_no_regrow`: unverified

> **Claim:** Unlike the hair cells of birds and amphibians, human hair cells don't grow back; most noise-induced hearing loss is caused by their damage and death.

- **Concept:** Hair cells in the cochlea (`concept.human_body.senses_cochlea_hair_cells`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L65 “How Ears Hear” · `card.human_body.065.c4` (fact): Your hair cells are not on the replacement list. / Unlike the hair cells of birds and amphibians, human hair cells don't grow back, and their damage and death cause most noise-induced hearing loss. Compare Level 10, where about 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day. The ones you hear with have to last.
- **Tested by:**
  - L65 `question.human_body.065.q3`: Level 10 said about 330 billion of your cells are replaced every day. What happens to your hearing's hair cells? → **Once they die, they don't grow back**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.smell_neurons_paths`: unverified

> **Claim:** Smell comes from olfactory sensory neurons in a small patch of tissue high inside the nose; odors reach them through the nostrils and, as you chew, through a channel from the roof of the throat to the nose.

Odors reach them two ways: through your nostrils and, as you chew, up a channel from the roof of your throat to your nose. Your brain blends those smells with the basic tastes, plus heat, cold and texture, into flavor. That's what tells a pear from an apple, and why a blocked nose leaves food flat.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: The Senses” · `card.human_body.070.c2` (text): Every sense, one trick / Every sense starts with specialized receptor cells that turn one kind of stimulus into a nerve signal, a step called transduction. - **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Arizona State University, Ask A Biologist: when we chew and swallow, odor molecules go up behind the palate through the back of the nasal cavity to odor receptors. Sources: https://askabiologist.asu.edu/smell-taste

### ☐ `fact.human_body.tongue_map_myth`: unverified

> **Claim:** The tongue map is a misconception: taste cells for different tastes are scattered across the tongue, and every area with taste buds senses all the basic tastes.

- **Concept:** Taste buds and the five basic tastes (`concept.human_body.senses_taste_basics`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L67 “Smell and Taste” · `card.human_body.067.c3` (fact): The 'tongue map' is a myth. / You may have seen a diagram with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back. In fact, taste cells for different tastes are scattered across the tongue, and every area with taste buds senses all the tastes. The map grew from a 1901 study that found only tiny differences in sensitivity, redrawn in the 1940s by Harvard psychologist Edwin Boring and read as separate zones.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Gizmodo ('Why did we believe in the tongue map?'): all areas of the tongue can detect all tastes; Virginia Collings's 1970s retest found the sensitivity differences made little to no practical difference. Sources: https://gizmodo.com/baffling-science-hoaxes-why-did-we-believe-in-the-tong-5927877

### ☐ `fact.human_body.voice_folds_vibrate`: unverified

> **Claim:** Voice is made by the vocal folds (vocal cords), two bands of tissue in the larynx: they are open for breathing and snap together, vibrating as air from the lungs blows past, when you speak.

- **Concept:** How the vocal folds make a voice (`concept.human_body.voice_vocal_folds`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L34 “Your Voice” · `card.human_body.034.c1` (text): Every word you've ever said was made of breath going out. / Level 33's diaphragm moves air in and out all day. Your voice borrows the outgoing half. So how does a plain stream of air become a laugh, a whisper or your own name?
  - L34 “Your Voice” · `card.human_body.034.c2` (text): Two folds in your voice box / Your voice box, the larynx, sits between the base of your tongue and the top of your windpipe. Inside it are the vocal folds (also called vocal cords), two bands of tissue. When you breathe, they stay open. When you speak, they snap together, and air from your lungs blowing past makes them vibrate. That buzz is your voice.
- **Tested by:**
  - L34 `question.human_body.034.q1`: What produces the sound of your voice? → **Vibrating vocal folds in the larynx**
  - L34 `question.human_body.034.q3`: Level 32 sent air past the voice box and down the windpipe. What are the vocal folds doing while you simply breathe? → **Staying open to let air through**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. NIDCD and Britannica agree: sound is produced by vibration of the vocal folds as exhaled air passes between them; NIDCD voice and speech text version adds the folds vibrate as air travels from the lungs. Sources: https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/news/multimedia/how-does-human-body-produce-voice-and-speech-text-version, https://www.britannica.com/science/vocal-cord

### ☐ `fact.human_body.capsaicin_trpv1`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the late 1990s, Julius used capsaicin, the chili pepper compound that causes a burning feeling, to find TRPV1, a sensor in nerve endings that is switched on by heat at temperatures felt as painful.

- **Appears in:**
  - L68 “Touch and Pain” · `card.human_body.068.c1` (text): A chili pepper tricks a heat sensor in your mouth. / The burn comes from a chemical, not a flame. Working out how it fools you earned a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize, and it shows how your skin turns touch, warmth and pain into signals.
  - L68 “Touch and Pain” · `card.human_body.068.c3` (text): A chili, a mint and a Nobel Prize / In the late 1990s, David Julius used capsaicin, the chemical that makes chilies burn, to find TRPV1, a sensor in nerve endings that switches on at painfully hot temperatures. Capsaicin flips the same switch. Julius and Ardem Patapoutian each used menthol to find a cold sensor, and Patapoutian found Piezo2, essential for touch and for Level 61's sense of body position. They shared the 2021 Nobel Prize.
- **Tested by:**

Without it, connective tissue weakens: tiredness, aching joints, swollen and bleeding gums, loose teeth, wounds that won't heal. Signs can appear within about a month, and untreated scurvy can kill. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.blood_color_oxygen`: unverified

> **Claim:** Blood that has just picked up oxygen is bright red; blood that has given up oxygen in the tissues is a darker, dusky red.

- **Concept:** Red blood cells carry oxygen (`concept.human_body.blood_red_cells`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L24 “What Blood Is Made Of” · `card.human_body.024.c3` (text): Red cells: the oxygen couriers / Red blood cells make up about 45 percent of blood's volume, and Level 3 found they are about 84 percent of all your cells. Their job is delivering oxygen from your lungs to your tissues. The carrier is hemoglobin, an iron-containing protein that also gives blood its color. Fresh from the lungs, blood is bright red; after dropping off oxygen, it's a duskier red. Never blue.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Heart and Blood” · `card.human_body.030.c2` (text): One lap, two circuits / Start in the left ventricle. One push sends your red cell out along an artery, branching smaller and smaller until it squeezes single file through a capillary and hands its oxygen to the tissues. Now a duskier red, it drifts home through the veins, with valves keeping it on course, into the right atrium. The right ventricle sends it to the lungs to reload, and it returns to the left side bright red again. One lap, two trips through the heart.
- **Tested by:**
  - L24 `question.human_body.024.q2`: Blood fresh from the lungs is bright red; blood coming back from the tissues is a duskier red. Why? → **It has given up oxygen to the tissues**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. LibreTexts composition of blood: oxygenated blood is bright red while deoxygenated blood is a darker, dusky red, because hemoglobin changes color with oxygen. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.capillary_exchange`: unverified

> **Claim:** Capillary walls are a single thin layer of cells, and through them oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between the blood and the tissues.

- **Concept:** Capillaries, where delivery happens (`concept.human_body.vessel_capillaries`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L23 “Blood Vessels” · `card.human_body.023.c2` (comparison): Three kinds of road: Arteries (Carry blood away from the heart; Thick walls; the big ones stretch with each push, then recoil) vs Veins (Carry blood back to the heart; Lower pressure, thinner walls; Many, especially in the limbs, have one-way valves) vs Capillaries (Link the smallest arteries to the smallest veins; Walls just one thin layer of cells)
  - L23 “Blood Vessels” · `card.human_body.023.c4` (text): Capillaries: where the delivery happens / Arteries and veins are only roads. The drop-off happens in capillaries, vessels so narrow (about 8 to 10 micrometers) that red blood cells squeeze through in single file. Their walls are a single thin layer of cells, so oxygen and nutrients cross out to your tissues and wastes cross in. All the pumping from Level 21 exists to get blood to this doorstep.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Heart and Blood” · `card.human_body.030.c2` (text): One lap, two circuits / Start in the left ventricle. One push sends your red cell out along an artery, branching smaller and smaller until it squeezes single file through a capillary and hands its oxygen to the tissues. Now a duskier red, it drifts home through the veins, with valves keeping it on course, into the right atrium. The right ventricle sends it to the lungs to reload, and it returns to the left side bright red again. One lap, two trips through the heart.
- **Tested by:**
  - L23 `question.human_body.023.q2`: Why do oxygen and nutrients leave the blood in capillaries, not in arteries? → **Capillary walls are one thin layer of cells**
  - L27 `question.human_body.027.q3`: Harvey couldn't see how blood crossed from arteries into veins. What did Malpighi's microscope reveal in 1661? → **Capillaries linking small arteries to small veins**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. SEER training module: capillary walls are a single layer of endothelial cells, where nutrients, oxygen and wastes are exchanged with the tissues. Sources: https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cardiovascular/blood/classification.html
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

  - L59 “Hormones and Feelings” · `card.human_body.059.c2` (text): Nerves text. Hormones broadcast. / Level 1 gave the endocrine system one job: sending hormones. Here's how they differ from nerves. Collagen, a tough protein, forms fibers that make bone flexible instead of brittle. Crystals of calcium phosphate harden around those fibers and make bone hard and strong. It's a bit like reinforced concrete: a hard material wrapped around a tough framework. Hard enough to hold you up, with just enough give to take a knock.

They're packed with collagen, the same tough protein that keeps bone from being brittle, and the fibers are lined up in parallel. Like the strands of a rope, parallel fibers resist stretching in the direction of the pull.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.fracture_healing_stages`: unverified

> **Claim:** Within hours of a fracture, blood clots around the break (about 6 to 8 hours); within about 48 hours a callus of cartilage starts bridging the gap; bone cells then replace the cartilage with spongy bone; finally compact bone forms and remodeling often leaves no trace of the break.

- **Appears in:**

### ☐ `fact.human_body.muscle_pairs_examples`: unverified

> **Claim:** The biceps bends (flexes) the elbow and the triceps on the back of the arm straightens (extends) it; the quadriceps straighten the knee and the hamstrings bend it.

So muscles work in pairs that pull in opposite directions. Your biceps pulls to bend your elbow; your triceps, on the back of your arm, pulls to straighten it. At the knee, the quadriceps straighten and the hamstrings bend. When one partner pulls, the other relaxes.
  - L16 “How Muscles Pull” · `card.human_body.016.c4` (text): Every push is a pull in disguise / So how do you push that door? Your triceps pulls to straighten your elbow, and your arm drives forward while the biceps relaxes. No muscle pushed anything. Every push you'll ever make is a pull happening somewhere else.

Oxygen passes through into the blood; carbon dioxide passes the other way.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.reflex_before_pain`: unverified

> **Claim:** When you touch a hot stove, you pull your hand away, typically before you have even registered the pain.

- **Concept:** The reflex arc (`concept.human_body.reflex_arc`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L53 “Reflexes” · `card.human_body.053.c1` (text): Touch a hot stove and your hand moves before you feel it. / You pull away, typically before you have even registered the pain. So who made the decision, if it wasn't the thinking you?
  - L53 “Reflexes” · `card.human_body.053.c2` (text): A shortcut through the spine / Sensors in your skin detect the heat. A signal races along a sensory fiber to your spinal cord, where it connects to a motor neuron. That neuron fires, your biceps contracts, and your hand is off the stove. Simple reflexes like this skip the brain's higher centers, the ones you use for deliberate moves. The spinal cord makes the call, and the brain gets the memo afterwards.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.fever_ancient`: unverified

> **Claim:** Fever has been conserved in warm- and cold-blooded vertebrates for over 600 million years.

- **Appears in:**
  - L74 “Fever” · `card.human_body.074.c5` (fact): Even cold-blooded lizards run a fever. / Fever has been part of fighting infection in warm- and cold-blooded animals for over 600 million years. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.harvey_calculation`: unverified

> **Claim:** Using cautious estimates of how much blood each beat pushes out, Harvey calculated that the heart pumps far more blood in a day than the whole body weighs, too much for the body to make from food and use up.

The heart, he found, pumps far more blood in a day than the whole body weighs. No body could make that much from food and use it all up. There was only one way out of the numbers: the same blood must be going round and round.

Search summary of Harvey accounts: Harvey assumed a minimum amount per beat and found the heart pumps several times a person's weight per hour, far more than the liver could make from food. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.allergy_ige_sensitization`: unverified

> **Claim:** In an allergy, IgE antibodies against the allergen attach to mast cells, sensitizing them to react the next time that allergen appears.

- **Concept:** How an allergy happens (`concept.human_body.defense_allergy_mechanism`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L79 “Allergies” · `card.human_body.079.c3` (text): Loaded first, triggered later / Allergies run on a kind of antibody called IgE. Once the immune system has made IgE against an allergen, those antibodies attach to mast cells and wait. That's called sensitization. The next time the allergen arrives, it binds to the IgE, and the mast cells release histamine, the chemical behind symptoms like a runny nose and swelling.   - L9 “How We Learned About the Body” · `card.human_body.009.c3` (timeline): Looking closer, then smaller: 1543: Vesalius's book maps the body from human dissection; 1665: Robert Hooke names 'cells' after the boxes he sees in cork; 1683: Leeuwenhoek describes bacteria from his own teeth; Late 1830s: Schleiden and Schwann: all living things are made of cells
  - L9 “How We Learned About the Body” · `card.human_body.009.c4` (text): Microbiology began with a set of teeth / Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own single lenses, magnifying up to about 300 times. In 1683 he looked at the plaque from his own teeth and saw 'little animalcules' moving about: bacteria, seen for the first time. The microbes you met in Level 8 had been living on people all along. It took a homemade lens to notice them.
  - L42 “Teeth” · `card.human_body.042.c4` (text): Hard, but not alive / Enamel is the hardest substance in your body, about 95 percent mineral by weight, mostly crystals of calcium phosphate. But once formed, it holds no living cells: the cells that built it are lost when the tooth comes in. So unlike bone, enamel can't remodel or regrow. It's also prime real estate. Level 9's Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria in the plaque from his own teeth.
  - L72 “Germs” · `card.human_body.072.c3` (text): The germ that slipped through the filter / Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria back in Level 9. Viruses were far too small for his lens. In 1892, Dmitry Ivanovsky found that a disease of tobacco plants passed through a filter fine enough to trap bacteria, so something smaller was carrying it. Most viruses measure from about 20 to a few hundred nanometers, and none can multiply outside a living cell. A virus is a set of instructions looking for a factory.
  - L97 “Surgery Then and Now” · `card.human_body.097.c3` (text): Surviving the operation, not the wound / Painless surgery still had a killer problem. In Joseph Lister's ward in Glasgow, 45 to 50 percent of amputation patients died of sepsis, an infection, between 1861 and 1865. After reading Louis Pasteur's germ theory, Lister concluded that microorganisms caused it, the same kind of tiny life Leeuwenhoek first spotted in Level 9. From 1865 he cleaned instruments and wounds with carbolic acid, and deaths in his ward fell sharply.
- **Tested by:**
  - L9 `question.human_body.009.q3`: Level 8's resident bacteria went unseen for most of history. Who first saw bacteria, and where? → **Leeuwenhoek, in plaque from his own teeth**
  - L10 `question.human_body.010.q5`: Building Blocks recap, from Level 9: what did Robert Hooke name after looking at cork through a lens? → **The cell**
  - L42 `question.human_body.042.q3`: Level 9's Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria. Where did he find them? → **In plaque from his own teeth**
  - L72 `question.human_body.072.q3`: Leeuwenhoek's lens revealed bacteria in Level 9. What 1892 finding showed viruses are smaller still? → **A tobacco disease that passed through a bacteria-trapping filter**
  - L97 `question.human_body.097.q3`: Level 9 met the first person to see bacteria. How does Leeuwenhoek's discovery connect to Lister's surgery? → **Lister fought the kind of microbes Leeuwenhoek first saw**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Royal Society and PMC histories: his 17 September 1683 letter described moving animalcules in plaque from his own teeth, the first undisputed description of bacteria. ### ☐ `fact.human_body.fracture_healing_timing`: unverified

> **Claim:** The clot forms over hours to days, the callus over days to weeks, and remodeling takes months to years; children go through the same stages much faster than adults.

- **Concept:** How a broken bone heals (`concept.human_body.fracture_healing`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L14 “Broken Bones” · `card.human_body.014.c3` (timeline): Four stages of bone repair: Within hours: Blood from torn vessels clots around the break; About 2 days: A callus of cartilage starts bridging the gap; Days to weeks: Bone cells replace the cartilage with spongy bone; Months to years: Compact bone forms and remodeling restores the shape
  - L14 “Broken Bones” · `card.human_body.014.c4` (text): Why a broken bone is kept still / Healing builds new bone around the pieces wherever they happen to be. A bone that isn't set back in line will heal in its bent position. That's why doctors put the pieces in place and use a cast or splint to keep the bone from moving while it heals. Children run through the same repair stages as adults, only much faster.
- **Tested by:**
  - L14 `question.human_body.014.q1`: What forms first at a broken bone, within hours of the break? → **A blood clot around the break**
  - L14 `question.human_body.014.q3`: Level 12 met spongy and compact bone. In what order do they form as a break heals? → **Spongy bone first, then compact bone**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Acibadem: hematoma in hours, soft callus 2 to 3 weeks, hard callus 3 to 12 weeks, remodeling for several years; OpenStax 6.5 gives a clot in 6 to 8 hours and callus within about 48 hours. Sources: https://acibademinternational.com/blog/fracture-healing-stages-explained-from-swelling-and-splint-to-follow-up-x-rays-and-rehab/, https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/6-5-fractures-bone-repair

The heart, he found, pumps far more blood in a day than the whole body weighs. No body could make that much from food and use it all up. There was only one way out of the numbers: the same blood must be going round and round.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.arm_third_class_lever`: unverified

> **Claim:** A bent arm is a Class 3 lever: the elbow is the pivot and the biceps pulls on the forearm closer to the elbow than the load; the muscle must pull harder than the load, but a small contraction gives a large, fast movement. Many muscle and bone combinations work this way.

- **Concept:** Bones and muscles as levers (`concept.human_body.musculoskeletal_levers`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L20 “Checkpoint: Bones and Muscles” · `card.human_body.020.c3` (text): Built for speed, not strength / Bend your arm. The elbow is the pivot, and the biceps pulls on the forearm closer to the elbow than the cup in your hand. That costs force: the muscle must pull harder than the load it lifts. In return, a small contraction swings your hand through a large, fast movement. Many of your muscle-and-bone pairs make the same trade.
- **Tested by:**
  - L20 `question.human_body.020.q2`: Bones and Muscles recap: the biceps pulls close to the elbow. What does the arm gain from that setup? → **A large, fast movement from a small contraction**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ABMP and Visible Body: third-class levers are the most common in the body; elbow flexion by the biceps favors speed and range of motion but needs force greater than the load. Sources: https://www.abmp.com/massage-and-bodywork-magazine/issues/julyaugust-2018/levers-human-body, https://www.visiblebody.com/blog/biomechanics-lever-systems-in-the-body

### ☐ `fact.human_body.nobel_1945_three`: unverified
