### ☐ `fact.human_body.oxford_bedpans`: unverified

> **Claim:** To make enough penicillin, the Oxford team grew the mold in all kinds of vessels, including hospital bedpans.

- **Concept:** Florey, Chain and the Oxford team (`concept.human_body.defense_penicillin_development`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L77 “Fleming and Penicillin” · `card.human_body.077.c1` (text): Penicillin was discovered in 1928. Its first patient came in 1941. / The famous part is a moldy dish and a lucky accident. The less famous part took a team in Oxford, a lot of glassware and even hospital bedpans. Both halves made the medicine.
  - L77 “Fleming and Penicillin” · `card.human_body.077.c4` (text): Oxford turns mold into medicine / In the late 1930s, Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team at Oxford isolated and purified penicillin, growing the mold in any vessel they could find, hospital bedpans included. In 1940, four infected mice given penicillin were alive hours later; four untreated mice were dead. In February 1941 a policeman became the first patient. He improved, then died when the supply ran out, even though they recovered penicillin from his urine.
- **Tested by:**
  - L77 `question.human_body.077.q2`: Why did penicillin wait until 1941 for its first patient? → **Nobody could purify and produce it until Florey and Chain's team did**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Oxford Health Histories: the team made more mould culture from bedpans and reclaimed penicillin from patient urine. Sources: https://oxfordhealth.web.ox.ac.uk/penicillin
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.human_body.dalton_dna_1995`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 1995, DNA from Dalton's preserved eye showed he lacked the gene for the medium-wavelength (green-sensitive) cone pigment.

- **Concept:** Color blindness (`concept.human_body.senses_color_blindness`)

  - L63 “Seeing Color” · `card.human_body.063.c4` (fact): Dalton blamed a blue tint inside his eyes. His own eye proved him wrong. / He guessed the jelly-like fluid in his eyes was tinted blue, and asked for them to be examined after his death. In 1844 they were: the fluid was colorless. In 1995, DNA from his preserved eye showed he lacked the gene for the green-sensitive cone pigment. He was right that his eyes differed, just wrong about why.

### ☐ `fact.human_body.gut_surface_2014`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 2014, Herbert Helander and Lars Fändriks used microscope measurements to find the digestive tract's inner surface is about 30 to 40 square meters in healthy adults, about half a badminton court.

- **Appears in:**

Then, in 2014, two scientists measured it properly. The real answer is smaller, but still big enough to explain how you absorb a meal.
  - L44 “The Intestines” · `card.human_body.044.c3` (fact): Your gut's inner surface is about 30 to 40 square meters: half a badminton court. / Herbert Helander and Lars Fändriks found that in 2014 using microscope measurements. Older textbooks said 180 to 300 square meters, a tennis court or more. Most of the real area is in the small intestine; the large intestine adds only about 2 square meters. Smaller than the legend, still roomy.
- **Tested by:**
  - L44 `question.human_body.044.q1`: What did a 2014 measurement find about the inner surface area of the digestive tract? → **It's about half a badminton court**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ScienceDaily (April 2014): quantitative microscopic techniques put the area at 30 to 40 square meters, half of a badminton court. Sources: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/04/140423111505.htm, https://medicalxpress.com/news/2014-04-surface-area-digestive-tract-large.html

Inside is an antigen: a killed or weakened form of the germ, a part of it, or genetic instructions (RNA or DNA) that tell your cells to make that part. Your immune system recognizes it, makes antibodies and remembers how to fight it. It learns the germ's face without meeting the germ at full strength.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Defending the Body” · `card.human_body.080.c2` (text): Four layers of defense / Layer one is the wall: dead, keratin-packed skin cells, replaced about every 4 weeks, on a dry, acidic surface. Layer two is innate immunity, the defense you're born with: phagocytes devour intruders, and fever's heat stirs white blood cells on. Layer three is acquired immunity: B cells, T cells and memory. Layer four is ours. Soap and water scrub germs away, vaccines train memory in advance, and penicillin blocks bacteria from building their cell walls.
- **Tested by:**
  - L75 `question.human_body.075.q1`: Which of these can a vaccine contain as its antigen? → **Genetic instructions to make part of a germ**
  - L75 `question.human_body.075.q3`: Why can a vaccine protect you from a germ you've never caught? → **It gives your immune system a first meeting, leaving memory cells**
  - L76 `question.human_body.076.q3`: Level 75 said vaccines train immunity without the disease. How did Jenner's cowpox fit that idea? → **Cowpox trained his defenses to resist smallpox without the disease**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. CDC Understanding How Vaccines Work: vaccines help the body learn to defend itself from disease without the dangers of a full-blown infection. Sources: https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/basics/explaining-how-vaccines-work.html
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.human_body.senses_aristotle_five`: unverified

> **Claim:** Aristotle listed five senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell) in his work De Anima (On the Soul) and argued there is no sixth.

- **Concept:** Senses beyond the classic five (`concept.human_body.senses_beyond_five`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L61 “More Than Five Senses” · `card.human_body.061.c2` (text): Aristotle's famous five / The classic list comes from Aristotle, the ancient Greek philosopher. In his book On the Soul (De Anima) he named sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell, and then argued there could be no sixth. The list stuck so well that it still feels like a law of nature. It's really a philosopher's tally, and tallies can be redone.
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica (Human sensory reception): "Aristotle described at least five senses"; Johnstone, 'Aristotle on the Unity of Touch', notes Aristotle argues explicitly in De Anima III.1 that there can be no more than five.
